title: Ten Years of Aided Phytostabilization in a Former Cu Mine: Evaluating Soil Recovery Under Different Amendment and Vegetation Strategies
content: Aided phytostabilization—combining soil amendments with tolerant vegetation—has proven effective improving soil properties and reducing potentially toxic elements (PTE) mobility in polluted soils, yet long-term studies are scarce. This study evaluates the 10-year evolution of an undergoing (aided) phytostabilization field trial at a former Cu mine in Touro (NW Spain), comparing different strategies for soil recovery and PTE immobilization. The mine soil (Spolic Technosol) was extremely acidic, nutrient-depleted, and virtually devoid of vegetation. Three amendments—compost (PC) and two technosols (PT1, PT2)—were assayed. Three planting treatments—Agrostis capillaris, AGR; Salix viminalis, SAL; unplanted, UNP—were established. Soil samples were collected before amendment applications and 1, 2, 3, 6 and 10 years after, then analyzed for pH, total C and N, POlsen, CECe and exchangeable cations, pseudo-total and readily available PTEs. All amendments immediately improved soil fertility and mitigated Cu availability (up to 3 orders of magnitude), thereby enabling vegetation establishment. Different amendments led to distinct initial trajectories that gradually converged toward a common pattern of long-term soil recovery. Aided phytostabilization effectively restored mine soil functionality for over a decade, but amendment choice should be aligned with site-specific recovery objectives and monitoring plans.
